candidates.attacker_control: The callback name is taken directly from the HTTP query string parameter `_jsonp` (or a configured alternative name); it is unauthenticated and fully attacker-controlled, URL-decoded by the JAX-RS query parser.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked that no validation exists anywhere in the JSONP package (searched for callback patterns/validation; none). Confirmed the sink writes bytes directly with no HTML/JS escaping, unlike other CXF response paths that escape (e.g. FormattedServiceListWriter uses StringEscapeUtils.escapeHtml4). Considered that the interceptors are opt-in (not auto-registered in bus-extensions.txt), which reduces affected deployments. Considered that a modern browser navigating directly to an application/x-javascript response usually displays text rather than executing it, so the practical XSS requires the JSONP response to be loaded as a script/gadget or sniffed; even then, arbitrary script text is injected. No tests are present in the snapshot to confirm intended behavior, and I could not verify against the upstream fix commit (no network/git history available).
candidates.impact: Cross-site scripting / script-content injection: an attacker can make victim browsers execute attacker-chosen JavaScript in the context of the origin that serves the JSONP endpoint (the injected callback is treated as code by any consumer that loads the URL as a script, e.g. `<script src="https://victim/app/rest?_jsonp=...">`), enabling session/data theft, CSRF token theft, or acting as a script gadget; where the browser content-sniffs the `application/x-javascript` response as HTML, the injected HTML is rendered directly. At minimum it is uncontrolled reflected script content (CWE-79/CWE-116) that would normally be prevented by a callback-name allow-list.
candidates.prerequisites: An application must register the JSONP interceptors (JsonpInInterceptor plus one of JsonpPreStreamInterceptor / JsonpJaxrsWriterInterceptor / the JSONP writer) so that a JSON-capable resource is served as JSONP. Response must not be cached as a static asset. The reflection itself then always occurs for any request containing the callback parameter.
candidates.root_cause: CXF's JSONP support accepts the callback function name from the request query string and never validates it against a safe JavaScript-identifier pattern (or escapes it). JsonpInInterceptor.getCallbackValue() reads `JAXRSUtils.getStructuredParams(queryString, "&", false, false).getFirst(callbackParam)` (callbackParam defaults to `_jsonp`) and stores the raw string under the exchange key `JSONP.CALLBACK`. The output-side interceptors then take that value and write it, unmodified, as the first bytes of the response body: JsonpPreStreamInterceptor writes `callback + "("` and JsonpJaxrsWriterInterceptor writes `callback + "("`, while the content type is forced to `application/x-javascript` (AbstractJsonpOutInterceptor.writeValue writes the string with UTF-8, no encoding). No component in the in/out path checks the value, so `?_jsonp=` can contain arbitrary JavaScript (including parentheses, quotes, `//`, or `</script>`-style HTML).
candidates.title: Unvalidated JSONP `_jsonp` callback value is reflected verbatim into an executable JavaScript response
candidates.trace: Request `GET /resource?_jsonp=<payload>` → JAXRSUtils query parsing in JsonpInInterceptor.getCallbackValue() (no validation) → exchange.put(JSONP.CALLBACK, payload) → out-bound JsonpPreStreamInterceptor.handleMessage()/JsonpJaxrsWriterInterceptor.aroundWriteTo() read the exchange value and write `payload + "("` to the response stream, setting Content-Type to application/x-javascript (JsonpPreStreamInterceptor.setContentType/context headers) → JSON payload appended → response body is attacker-prefixed script.
candidates.unverified: Not runtime-verified (no code execution permitted). The exact upstream fix/version impact and the CVE mapping are unverified. Whether a specific deployment enables the JSONP interceptors and how its browser/consumer handles the script content type determines real-world exploitability. Whether clients of this snapshot treat the reflected value as a security boundary is also unverified.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-79 / CWE-116 (Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation; unsafe reflection of attacker input into script output)

coverage_summary: Read-only review of the assigned Apache CXF 3.5.9 snapshot (5,171 files, 4,154 Java files; tests are absent from the snapshot). I inspected: core StaxUtils/attachment/URIResolver/resource handling; JAX-RS front end (JAXRSUtils, RequestPreprocessor, providers incl. JSONP/XSLT/SourceProvider, multipart handling); JAX-RS extensions (search/FIQL, providers, description WADL/Swagger/OpenAPI); HTTP transports (servlet, Undertow, Netty, Jetty, headers/TLS); WS-Security/WSS4J policy validators, STS/JWT validators; JOSE/JWS/JWE/JWK, OAuth2, OIDC, SSO/SAML and CORS; WSDL manager/locator; JMS transport URI/JNDI handling; JMS SOAP binding interceptor; WS-Addressing/WS-RM/WS-Discovery/MEX spot checks; samples and build/config files. Coverage is broad but not exhaustive; no runtime, test, scanner, or dependency-level analysis was performed.
limitations: No test sources exist in the snapshot, so intended security behavior could not be confirmed by tests and no regression tests are available.
No git history, tags, or fix commits are available, so I could not diff this snapshot against the upstream fix or confirm which CVE (if any) is present; no network access was used.
No code was executed, no scanners were run, so findings are static and not runtime-confirmed.
The repository is large (5,171 files); several subsystems (WS-RM persistence, CORBA binding, tools/codegen, OSGi/JCA integration, maven plugins, most samples) were only spot-checked.

The chosen candidate's exploitability depends on deployment (registration of the JSONP interceptors) and on how a consumer/browser handles an application/x-javascript response, which I could not verify at runtime.

rejected_leads.lead: Swagger UI resource path handling (SwaggerUiService.getResource `{resource:.*}` -> SwaggerUiResourceLocator.locate concatenating resourcePath into URI.create(root+path)) allows `..` segments, but the root is always produced by SwaggerUiResolver/OsgiSwaggerUiResolver as a `jar:`/bundle-entry URL, so traversal outside the jar is not achievable; judged not exploitable.
rejected_leads.reason: No attacker-reachable file/dir root; jar entry lookup does not resolve `..`.

rejected_leads.lead: Undertow transport error page (UndertowHTTPHandler lines 129-131) writes `t.getMessage()` unescaped into a `text/html` 500 page.
rejected_leads.reason: Concrete unescaped HTML sink, but attacker control requires an exception whose message embeds request data to propagate to this catch block; the normal CXF/JAX-RS error handling converts most input-derived failures into responses, so the chain could not be established from source alone.

rejected_leads.lead: Distributed sample apps contain clear vulnerabilities: `distribution/.../samples/jax_rs/search/.../Catalog.addBook` uses the multipart attachment filename (`handler.getName()`) as a file name in `Storage.addDocument` -> `new File(folder, name)` (path traversal/file write), and `distribution/.../samples/ws_eventing/.../EarthquakeEventServlet` / `FireEventServlet` write `request.getParameter("location")` unescaped into HTML.
rejected_leads.reason: These are demo/sample applications shipped alongside the product, not the runtime library; I selected the library-code finding. They remain real defects if the sample is deployed.

rejected_leads.lead: CORS filter (CrossOriginResourceSharingFilter) echoes any request Origin with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` when `allowCredentials` is configured while the origin allow-list is empty/allow-all.
rejected_leads.reason: Configuration-dependent behavior that follows the CORS spec (wildcard cannot be used with credentials); it requires the deployer to set allowCredentials with an empty allowOrigins list, so it is a hardening/config issue rather than a clear vulnerability.

rejected_leads.lead: MaskSensitiveHelper builds regex replacement patterns from configured sensitive element names via String.replaceAll and matches content types by substring (`contains("xml")` etc.).
rejected_leads.reason: Inputs are application configuration, not attacker-controlled; failures only affect log masking. Hardening opportunity, not a vulnerability.

rejected_leads.lead: JWS JSON verification uses the JWS `unionHeader` (protected + unprotected headers) for algorithm/id matching (JwsJsonSignatureEntry.verifySignatureWith, JwsJsonConsumer).
rejected_leads.reason: Verifier implementations pin the algorithm and its family (PublicKeyJwsSignatureVerifier.checkAlgorithm requires RSA and equality with the configured algorithm; HMAC requires HMAC), and header-supplied JWK acceptance defaults to false, so no algorithm-confusion path was demonstrable. Verified the x5c path performs PKIX chain validation against the configured trust store.

rejected_leads.lead: WSDL/`?xsd=`/`?wsdl` handling as an SSRF/LFI vector (WSDLGetUtils, WSDLManagerImpl, ResourceManagerWSDLLocator).
rejected_leads.reason: WSDL import locations are checked against an ALLOWED_SCHEMES allow-list (file/http/https/classpath/jar) in AbstractWrapperWSDLLocator, and `?xsd=` is resolved only through already-known SchemaReference map entries (lookupSchemaReference throws SCHEMA_NOT_FOUND otherwise).

summary: Apache CXF 3.5.9 snapshot (~4,150 Java files, tests stripped). I reviewed the request-handling surface (JAX-RS/JAX-WS front ends, HTTP transports, attachments/multipart, WSDL/WADL/Swagger endpoints, CORS, JOSE/JWT, OAuth2, SAML/STS, JMS, XML parsing). The core XML/parsing hardening (StaxUtils XXE/DTD/entity protections), the WSDL-import scheme allow-list (AbstractWrapperWSDLLocator.ALLOWED_SCHEMES), XOP follow-URLs default-off, and JWS algorithm-family pinning are present and correct, so several classic CXF CVE areas are already fixed in this snapshot. The single strongest un-mitigated source-level issue I could trace is the JSONP support: the attacker-controlled `_jsonp` query parameter is stored in the exchange and then written verbatim into the response body as executable JavaScript with a script content type, with no validation/encoding at any point (CWE-79/CWE-116). I am submitting that one candidate; other leads are listed as rejected/unconfirmed.
